title: karma — the Isha Upanishad as a life

segments.voice: Yesterday: karma, and the Isha's first verse. All this is dwelt in by the Lord; enjoy by letting go; whose is wealth? Did you use something as if you'd borrowed it? Today, the second verse, and the work itself. Day six hundred ninety-one.

If the first verse of the Isha had stopped at renounce and don't covet, you might expect the next line to say: so leave. Go to the forest. Stop working. It says the opposite. The very next verse tells you to keep doing your work, and to want to live a hundred years doing it. For anyone with a job, a family and a to-do list that never ends, that's a line worth hearing slowly.
screen: `AFTER RENOUNCE, YOU'D EXPECT: LEAVE.` → `IT SAYS: KEEP WORKING.` → `FOR A HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Verse two begins: kurvann eveha karmani, doing works here, indeed. Jijivishet shatam samah, one may wish to live a hundred years. Then the turn. For you, thus, and not otherwise: na karma lipyate nare. Action does not cling to the person. Lipyate is the word for something smeared on, sticking. The picture is of work that doesn't leave a stain. How? Because of the first verse. If you act in a world you don't own, without coveting its results, the action passes through you instead of sticking to you. Shankara reads this verse as a concession for those not yet ready to renounce: if you must act, act this way. Other teachers hear it as a whole path in itself, close to what the Bhagavad Gita teaches about acting without attachment to results. The Gita even uses the same verb for a lotus leaf that water doesn't stick to. Then, a few verses on, the Isha says something sharper. Those who follow avidya, ignorance, or in one reading ritual action alone, enter blinding darkness. Those who delight only in vidya, knowledge, enter a greater darkness still. And whoever knows both together crosses death by the one and reaches the deathless by the other. The commentators argue about exactly what the two words mean here. One common way to hear it: action without understanding is dark, and understanding that refuses to act is darker. Read that way, the Isha asks for both, held at once. So the life the Isha imagines isn't a monk's and isn't a busy person's. It's someone who does a full day's work, wants to keep doing it for a long time, and somehow doesn't get stuck to it.
screen: `DO YOUR WORK; WISH FOR A HUNDRED YEARS.` · `NA KARMA LIPYATE: ACTION DOESN'T CLING.` · `ACTION ALONE, KNOWING ALONE: DARK.` · `BOTH TOGETHER.` · then, large: `WORK THAT LEAVES NO STAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle the breath. Think of one piece of work waiting for you today: a task, a chore, an email. Picture yourself doing it well, fully, with care. Then picture finishing it and setting it down, not checking who noticed, not replaying how it went. Just done, and released. Let the breath move through like water over a lotus leaf. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action. The Isha says do your work, wish to live a hundred years doing it, and the action won't cling.
Your line: work that leaves no stain. Today, do one task completely, then let it go without grabbing at the result. Day six hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Hindus on the path of karma yoga often describe their work, at home, in a job or in service, as an offering done without clinging to its results, and some teachers cite the Isha's second verse alongside the Bhagavad Gita for this.

match.prompt: the second verse and after — tap the pairs.

myth: the Isha tells its reader to stop working and leave the world
verse two says keep doing your work, and wish to live a hundred years.
the Isha says knowledge that refuses action leads to a greater darkness
those who delight only in vidya enter a darkness greater still.
all commentators read verse two the same way
Shankara reads it as a concession; other teachers as a full path.

fork.setup: you've just read: renounce, and don't covet. you have a demanding job and a family. what does the Isha's next verse say?
options: quit and go to the forest.
keep working, wish for a hundred years, and action won't cling.
fork.reveal: kurvann eveha karmani: doing works here. act in a world you don't own, and the action doesn't stick.

original.note: Sanskrit, Isha 2: na (not) karma (action) lipyate (clings) nare (to a person). action does not cling to the person.

trapdoor: what you thought: spiritual life means stepping away from work.
what it means: the Isha says work fully, for a long life, without the grip that makes action stick.

what a scholar hears: lipyate, 'is smeared,' is the same image the Gita uses for the lotus leaf untouched by water (Gita 5.10); Isha 9–11 on vidya and avidya is read differently by Shankara and later teachers.

sources.ref: Shankara's commentary on Isha Upanishad 2 and 9–11
Bhagavad Gita 2.47; 5.10 (action without attachment; the lotus leaf)

notes: Quotation is the Sanskrit original (transliterated): 'na karma lipyate nare'. Confirm.
Shankara's reading of verse 2 as for those unable to renounce, and of avidya as ritual works and vidya as meditation on deities, should be checked.

Reviewer: the 'action dark, knowledge darker' reading of Isha 9–11 is now framed as one common interpretation, since Shankara takes vidya as meditation on deities rather than knowledge in general. The Gita is 'usually dated later' rather than 'centuries later', since relative dating is debated. The myth item 'knowledge that refuses action leads to a greater darkness' leans on that interpretation; confirm wording.
The lotus-leaf image in the practice anticipates Gita 5.10; the verb there is lipyate as well. Confirm.
Day 692 (another writer) picks up with 'what did you do yesterday without grabbing at the result?', which this carry sets up.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the superlative 'one of the most practical lines in the Upanishads'; fixed the claim that the Gita 'hears' the Isha verse a certain way (the Gita doesn't comment on the Isha) to 'close to what the Gita teaches'; set up the practice's lotus-leaf image in the teach (Gita 5.10 uses lipyate); 'many teachers/others' softened in howItsDone and myth.
